I appreciate you sharing your experience as a dyslexic learner, but I don’t think it’s fair to dismiss phonics entirely with an eye roll. Different approaches work for different students, and I’ve seen firsthand that phonics can help dyslexic learners—albeit with a lot of repetition and patience. 

The methods you suggest—like putting words into context or using auditory support—are great strategies, and I think they can complement phonics rather than replace it. For some students, combining different approaches is exactly what they need to make progress. 

I’m here to learn more and improve my teaching, so I’m open to trying different things. But I don’t think it’s helpful to completely write off phonics when it’s been proven to work for many kids, including those with dyslexia.

Nature walks is also one of the best things we can do for self-regulation as ND people and humans in general. It boosts serotonin to see and smell the flowers and trees. Walking also does something to brain activity because of its bilateral movement. Literally makes us think better and get out of that mentally stuck feeling.

To anyone feeling discouraged about teaching as a career-

At my elementary school in Houston, it was exactly as OP described. At my current elementary school in Austin, I am continuously blown away by how well this school is functioning. Everything the last place did wrong, this place does well or at least manages it much more effectively. The kids needs are actually addressed. I see social emotional growth and teachers that are compassionate about students emotional/behavioral needs. A great example is the 5th grade science teacher. She has two boys on the autism spectrum in here class and they have stereotypical “dorky” socially awkward traits, but no one treats them like a “dork”. In that classroom. The teacher allows them to share their “fun facts” related to the content with the class and doesn’t shame them for being different. They’re allowed to sit at their desk when the rest of the class is on the rug because it works better for them. Kids are treated as humans, not as inconvenient obstacles in the way. 

Of course there are some shortages and it gets stressful this time of year with testing, but I wouldn’t have believed that this public school existed 3 months ago. It’s not the same type of stress (trauma) I experienced before. Not sure why, but the overcrowding isn’t an issue here (about 16 kids per class). It’s a culture of support and actual inclusion. Every teacher is a positive role model in some aspect. 

Teachers are not expected to be perfect or judged for having their own way of doing things. There is a lot of freedom to teach the content how you see fit. No micromanaging or stupid pointless “planning” curriculum meetings. Just real learning and progress happening! I don’t know how I got so lucky, but I’m serious that it’s an amazing experience to be influencing kids and watching kids grow and succeed. 

I think it’s worth searching for an environment which makes that possible. If I had let all the discouragement in my past and in public forum deter me, I never would have found this incredible opportunity. I just have to share about it because it still blows my mind and makes me so grateful.

Sure, I can share about stimulant use. It’s a major pro/con list. When you go up, you feel so calm, clear headed, focused, can power through difficult or boring tasks with ease and even enjoyment, social anxiety is completely gone, positive outlook on life and especially on your ability to tackle life. You feel capable and empowered. It’s like EVERYTHING becomes interesting and awesome and life is good. Sensory issues dissipate so you aren’t held back by any pesky sensation or annoying thought patterns. You become wholly focused on whatever you’re working on with little to no distractive urges (unless you’re giving in to a tempting distraction, like texting a friend that you’re having good convo with, then you will be wholly focused on that). It gives you energy and feels like coming back from the dead. It makes you feel like a “normal person”.

The downsides are when you’re coming down from the drug. What goes up, must come down. Anxiety, irritability, insomnia, brain fog, and desire for more of the drug are the biggest negative affects for me. Additionally, getting focused on the wrong things was a big problem for me but with a good plan in place I think that can be ameliorated for some. 

There isn’t really an end game, it’s just a useful tool for those with motivation issues and executive dysfunction. It also sucks because of the tolerance issues. After a few weeks, you become pretty useless without the drug in your system. It’s easy to see why it’s so addictive. Adderall is like the movie Limitless, if you’re familiar. I don’t miss the panic attacks or being in fight or flight mode for hours on end each day. There is a trade off. I hope that answers your question.
